analysis.one_liner: Gives Americans legal rights over their personal data and restricts how companies collect and sell it.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan House privacy bill backed by the Energy and Commerce chair and the committee's top Democrat never received a committee vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give people nationwide the right to see, correct, delete, and take with them the personal data companies hold about them. It would require companies to collect only the data they actually need, get clear permission before handling sensitive information like health records, precise location, biometrics, and private messages, and ban the sale of biometric and genetic data outright. It adds special protections for children and teens, requires plain-language privacy policies, and lets the Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and in narrow cases individuals enforce the rules. Small businesses under $40 million in revenue are exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users. Anyone who uses apps, websites, phones, or connected devices would gain enforceable rights over their data, and parents would gain new controls over what companies collect from children and teenagers. People are especially protected on the most sensitive categories: health conditions, precise location, biometric identifiers, genetic data, private messages, and even neural data.

how_it_helps.text: Companies could only collect, keep, and share data that is 'necessary, proportionate, and limited' to providing the service a person asked for or another specifically permitted purpose.

Individuals would gain the right to access, correct, delete, and export the data a company holds on them, with responses required within 30 days for large data holders and data brokers and 45 days for others; the first three requests per year are free.
Transferring sensitive data to third parties would require the person's clear, affirmative consent, and biometric and genetic information could never be transferred for payment or anything of value.
Covered entities include common carriers and nonprofits, not just traditional FTC-jurisdiction firms, so telephone and internet carriers are covered alongside websites and apps.

The bill would require large data holders (roughly $250 million or more in annual revenue with millions of users) to publish easy-to-read privacy policies and keep a public log of every change for ten years.
Enforcement would come from three directions: the FTC, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits in limited circumstances.

analysis.who_pays: Large data companies: social media platforms, advertising-technology firms, and data brokers would bear compliance costs and lose revenue from unrestricted collection and resale of personal data, especially targeted advertising built on tracking people across sites. Some of those costs could reach consumers through prices or ad-supported services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big tech, ad-tech, and data brokers

drawbacks.text: Private lawsuits are limited to a defined 'substantial privacy harm' — financial harm of at least $10,000, or serious physical or mental harm such as injury or highly offensive intrusion. A person whose data was misused in an ordinary way with no provable $10,000 loss could not sue, so most enforcement would depend on the FTC and state attorneys general.
The bill would terminate the FTC's pending rulemaking on commercial surveillance and data security, replacing an in-progress agency process with whatever the statute itself provides.

The bill's 'Relation to other laws' section would set one national standard in place of the current patchwork of state privacy rules; if the federal floor ended up weaker than laws some states have already passed, people in those states could lose protections they have today.

Compliance would be costly for covered companies, and businesses with under $40 million in revenue are fully exempt, which leaves a large slice of the app and website economy outside the rules' reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For individuals, the rights granted are substantial and the direct cost to them is essentially none; the strongest honest objections are design ones, not the goal. Weak private enforcement, the end of the FTC's surveillance rulemaking, and unresolved state preemption mean the bill would rely heavily on federal and state regulators to do its work, and the question of whether it would override stronger state laws like California's was the most contested design issue. The core protections — consent for sensitive data, a ban on selling biometric and genetic data, and real rights to delete and export data — are meaningful and would have applied nationwide.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled a markup or vote on it, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Cathy McMorris Rodgers introduced the American Privacy Rights Act of 2024 on June 25, 2024, joined as original cosponsors by Representatives Frank Pallone, Gus Bilirakis, and Jan Schakowsky — the Energy and Commerce Committee's chair and ranking member among them.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction.
No further action was ever taken: no subcommittee or full committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion activity appears in the bill's action history.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, advertising-technology companies, and large platforms came out ahead: the data-collection and targeted-advertising practices the bill would have restricted continued unregulated at the federal level, and Americans gained no new privacy rights. Consumers, and regulators who had pushed for a national standard, came out with nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four named backers split evenly, two Republicans and two Democrats, and included both the chair and ranking member of the committee that would have considered it.

industries.note: Data brokers make their principal revenue processing and transferring data they did not collect directly from the people it describes. The bill would subject them to deadlines on deletion and access requests, require companies to disclose by name which data brokers they sell to, and ban transferring data to brokers for many sensitive purposes. People gain control over data that is currently bought and sold without their knowledge.

Targeted advertising under the bill would be limited to data already collected lawfully, excluded for anyone who opts out, and banned entirely for children and teens, with universal opt-out mechanisms required. This directly constrains the cross-site tracking that funds much of the free internet's advertising business.

industries.industry: Large technology platforms and social media companies
industries.note: Companies with $3 billion or more in global revenue and 300 million or more users face heightened duties, and large data holders ($250 million-plus revenue with millions of users) must publish short-form notices and decade-long logs of privacy policy changes. The compliance and liability burden falls on the biggest firms, some of which may pass costs to users through ads or prices.

Collecting or processing biometric or genetic information would require affirmative express consent, and transferring it for payment or anything of value would be prohibited outright. Firms built on monetizing faces, voices, fingerprints, or DNA would lose that market.
